# term<TAB>meaning. Several spellings can share one meaning: "term1|term2<TAB>meaning".

column2: A system where power is divided between the Union (Centre) and the States by the Constitution. India is a "Union of States" (Art. 1): federal in structure but with a strong Centre and unitary features (single citizenship, All India Services, emergency powers), so it is often called quasi-federal.
Federal in form but with a strong unitary bias, as K.C. Wheare described India: the Centre has more powers, can form or alter States (Art. 3) and takes over in emergencies.

A system where all power rests with one central government. India's Constitution has unitary features (single Constitution, single citizenship, integrated judiciary, emergency provisions) within a federal structure.
Free to decide its own internal and external affairs, not subject to any outside authority. The Preamble declares India a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic.

In the Preamble (added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976): India's goal of ending inequality of income, status and opportunity through a mixed economy - "democratic socialism", not state ownership of everything.

In the Indian sense (added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment, 1976): the State has no religion of its own and treats all religions equally ("sarva dharma sambhava"), rather than keeping fully separate from religion as in the West.
Government by elected representatives of the people with universal adult franchise; in India it covers political, social and economic democracy.
A State whose head is elected, not hereditary. India's President is elected indirectly for five years.

The introduction to the Constitution, based on Nehru's Objectives Resolution (1946). It states the source of authority (We, the People), the nature of the State and its objectives (justice, liberty, equality, fraternity). Part of the Constitution (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) but not enforceable in court.
The supreme law of India, adopted on 26 November 1949 and in force from 26 January 1950, framed by the Constituent Assembly.
The body that framed India's Constitution (1946-49), set up under the Cabinet Mission Plan; Dr Rajendra Prasad was President and Dr B.R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee.
Basic rights in Part III (Arts. 12-35) of the Constitution, enforceable in courts (Art. 32, Art. 226); the State cannot take them away except as the Constitution allows.
Duties of citizens in Part IVA (Art. 51A), added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice; now 11. Not enforceable in court.

column1: directive principles|dpsp|directive principles of state policy
column2: Guidelines for the State in Part IV (Arts. 36-51) to build a welfare State, taken from the Irish Constitution. Not enforceable in court but "fundamental in the governance of the country" (Art. 37).

The doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) that Parliament may amend any part of the Constitution but cannot destroy its basic features, such as supremacy of the Constitution, federalism, secularism and judicial review.
The power of the Supreme Court and High Courts to strike down laws and executive actions that go against the Constitution; part of the basic structure.
A court order to enforce rights. The Supreme Court (Art. 32) and High Courts (Art. 226) can issue habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.
To have the body: a writ ordering a person who has been detained to be produced before the court, so the court can check whether the detention is lawful.
We command: a writ ordering a public official or body to do a duty it has failed to do.
A writ by which a higher court quashes an order of a lower court or tribunal passed without jurisdiction or in error.
By what authority: a writ asking a person to show by what right they hold a public office.
(As a writ) an order of a higher court stopping a lower court or tribunal from going beyond its jurisdiction.
A temporary law made by the President (Art. 123) or a Governor (Art. 213) when the legislature is not in session; it lapses six weeks after the legislature reassembles unless approved.
A Bill only on taxes, borrowing and the Consolidated Fund (Art. 110). It can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha; the Speaker certifies it, and the Rajya Sabha can only delay it for 14 days.
A Bill on revenue or expenditure that is not purely a Money Bill; it needs the President's recommendation and follows the ordinary procedure in the Rajya Sabha.

A sitting of both Houses of Parliament called by the President (Art. 108) to settle a deadlock on an ordinary Bill; the Speaker presides. Not allowed for Money Bills or Constitutional Amendment Bills.
The time right after Question Hour in Parliament when members raise urgent matters without prior notice; an Indian innovation (1962), not in the Rules.
The first hour of a sitting of Parliament, when members ask ministers questions (starred - oral; unstarred - written answers; short notice).
A motion in the Lok Sabha that the Council of Ministers has lost the House's support; needs 50 members to admit it, and if passed the government must resign (Art. 75: collective responsibility).
A motion criticising particular policies or actions of the government; it must state reasons, and passing it does not force the government to resign.
A motion in the Lok Sabha to set aside normal business and discuss an urgent matter of public importance; needs 50 members' support.
A party official, and the written order they issue, telling party MPs or MLAs how to vote; defying it can lead to disqualification under the Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule).
The Tenth Schedule (52nd Amendment, 1985): MPs and MLAs who leave their party or defy its whip can be disqualified by the Speaker/Chairman; merger of two-thirds of a party is exempt.
Central rule in a State under Art. 356 when its government cannot be run as per the Constitution; approved by Parliament within two months, for up to three years. Limited by S.R. Bommai (1994).
Special powers in Part XVIII: National Emergency (Art. 352: war, external aggression, armed rebellion), President's Rule (Art. 356) and Financial Emergency (Art. 360, never used).

The constitutional head of a State, appointed by the President for five years (holds office at the President's pleasure); acts on the advice of the State Council of Ministers except in discretionary matters.
The presiding officer of the Lok Sabha (or a State Assembly), elected by its members; decides whether a Bill is a Money Bill and on disqualification under the Tenth Schedule.
The Government of India's chief legal adviser (Art. 76), appointed by the President; may speak in Parliament but cannot vote.
The auditor of all receipts and spending of the Union and States (Art. 148), appointed by the President for six years or until age 65; called the guardian of the public purse.
A body set up by the President every five years (Art. 280) to recommend how taxes are shared between the Centre and the States and grants-in-aid to States.
The constitutional body (Art. 324) that conducts elections to Parliament, State legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President.
The three-tier system of rural local self-government (village, block, district) given constitutional status by the 73rd Amendment (1992), Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule (29 subjects).
All registered voters of a village panchayat area; under PESA it has special powers over land, resources and customs in Scheduled Areas.
An urban local body; the 74th Amendment (1992) gave them constitutional status (Part IXA, Twelfth Schedule, 18 subjects).
Communities notified by the President under Art. 341 as having suffered untouchability; given reservations and protection under the Constitution.
Tribal communities notified by the President under Art. 342; protected through reservations and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules.
Tribal areas declared by the President under the Fifth Schedule, with a Tribes Advisory Council and special powers for the Governor.
Seats kept aside in legislatures, education and government jobs for SCs, STs, OBCs and EWS (Arts. 15(4), 16(4), 330, 332); capped at 50% by the Indra Sawhney case (1992), except EWS.
The better-off section of the OBCs who are excluded from reservation benefits (Indra Sawhney, 1992), set by an income limit.

Dual government: introduced in the provinces by the Government of India Act 1919 (reserved subjects under the Governor, transferred subjects under Indian ministers) and planned at the Centre by the 1935 Act.
Same as dyarchy: dual government, introduced in the provinces by the Government of India Act 1919.
The British Crown's supreme authority over the Indian princely states, which lapsed in 1947 when they could join India or Pakistan.
Lord Dalhousie's policy (1848-56) of annexing a princely state when its ruler died without a natural heir (adopted heirs were not recognised); Satara, Jhansi and Nagpur were taken.
Lord Wellesley's system (1798): Indian rulers kept a British army at their own cost and a British Resident at court and could not deal with other powers; Hyderabad was the first to accept.
Cornwallis's land revenue system (1793) in Bengal, Bihar and Odisha: zamindars became owners and paid a fixed revenue to the Company forever.
A land revenue system (Thomas Munro, Madras; also Bombay) where the cultivator (ryot) paid revenue directly to the government.
A land revenue system (Holt Mackenzie, 1822; North-West Provinces, Punjab) where revenue was fixed on the whole village (mahal), collected through the headman.
Of one's own country: the movement (from 1905, against the partition of Bengal) to use Indian goods and boycott British ones.
Gandhi's method of non-violent resistance - "insistence on truth" - first used in South Africa and then at Champaran (1917).
Gandhi's movement (1930-34), begun with the Dandi Salt March, of openly breaking unjust laws non-violently.
The fourfold division of Vedic society: Brahmana, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra.
A hereditary caste group based on birth and occupation, the working unit of the caste system.
The assemblies of Tamil poets at Madurai under Pandya patronage, which produced the Sangam literature (about 300 BCE - 300 CE).
The dynasty that ruled the Deccan, including Andhra, after the Mauryas (about 1st century BCE - 3rd century CE); capitals at Pratishthana and Amaravati/Dhanyakataka.

The seasonal reversal of winds that brings India most of its rain: the South-West monsoon (June-September) and the retreating North-East monsoon (October-December), which rains on Tamil Nadu and coastal Andhra.
The crop season sown with the South-West monsoon (June-July) and harvested in September-October: rice, maize, cotton, groundnut, jowar.
The crop season sown in October-November and harvested in March-April: wheat, gram, mustard, barley.
The short summer crop season between rabi and kharif (March-June): watermelon, cucumber, fodder crops.
The land between two rivers that meet, such as the Ganga-Yamuna doab or the Krishna-Tungabhadra (Raichur) doab.
The Western and Eastern Ghats: the mountain ranges along India's west and east coasts; also steps leading down to a river.
Salt-tolerant forests of tidal coasts and deltas; in Andhra Pradesh at the Godavari and Krishna deltas (Coringa).
A large protected area under UNESCO's Man and the Biosphere programme with a core, buffer and transition zone; India has 18 (Seshachalam in Andhra Pradesh).
A protected area where no human activity like grazing or private rights is allowed, declared under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972.
A protected area for wildlife where some human activities (like grazing) may be permitted, under the Wildlife Protection Act 1972.
A protected area for tigers under Project Tiger (1973), notified under the Wildlife Protection Act; Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam is India's largest.
A general rise in prices over time. In India it is measured mainly by the Consumer Price Index (CPI); the RBI targets 4% CPI inflation (band of 2-6%).
The rate at which the RBI lends short-term money to banks against government securities; the main tool of monetary policy, set by the Monetary Policy Committee.
The rate at which the RBI borrows money from banks; since 2022 the Standing Deposit Facility is the floor of the policy corridor.
The share of a bank's deposits that it must keep as cash with the RBI, earning no interest.
The share of a bank's deposits that it must keep in cash, gold or government securities itself.
The government's total borrowing need in a year: total expenditure minus revenue receipts and non-debt capital receipts. The FRBM target for the Centre is 3% of GDP.
Revenue expenditure minus revenue receipts: shows how much the government borrows to meet day-to-day spending.
Fiscal deficit minus interest payments: the borrowing needed apart from paying interest on past debt.
The value of all final goods and services produced within the country in a year. India's base year is 2011-12 (being revised).
The single indirect tax on goods and services across India since 1 July 2017 (101st Amendment), with CGST, SGST and IGST; rates are set by the GST Council.
The Annual Financial Statement (Art. 112): the government's estimated receipts and spending for the financial year (1 April - 31 March), presented in Parliament.
The main account of the Government of India (Art. 266): all revenues, loans and loan repayments go into it, and no money can be spent from it without Parliament's approval.
A fund placed at the President's disposal (Art. 267) for urgent unforeseen spending, made good later by Parliament.
The account (Art. 266(2)) for money the government holds as a banker, such as provident funds and small savings, which does not need Parliament's vote.
National Institution for Transforming India: the government's policy think tank, set up on 1 January 2015 to replace the Planning Commission; the Prime Minister is its Chairperson.
The body (1950-2014) that made India's Five-Year Plans, set up by a Cabinet resolution; replaced by NITI Aayog.
India's development plans from 1951 to 2017, made by the Planning Commission; the 12th Plan (2012-17) was the last.
The price at which the government promises to buy certain crops from farmers, announced for 22 crops on the advice of the Commission for Agricultural Costs and Prices (CACP).
The rise in food grain output from the late 1960s through high-yielding seeds, fertilisers and irrigation, led by M.S. Swaminathan, mainly in wheat in Punjab, Haryana and western UP.
Operation Flood (from 1970) led by Verghese Kurien, which made India the world's largest milk producer.
The growth of fisheries and aquaculture; Andhra Pradesh is India's leading producer of farmed fish and shrimp.
A small group of 10-20 poor people, mostly women, who save together and take bank loans as a group; linked to banks under NABARD's programme (1992) and DAY-NRLM.

column2: The 2005 Act that guaranteed 100 days of paid unskilled work a year to every rural household that asked for it; replaced from 1 July 2026 by VB-G RAM G.
Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act 1996: extends Panchayati Raj to Fifth Schedule tribal areas with strong powers for the Gram Sabha.
The House of the People: the lower House of Parliament, directly elected, with 543 elected seats; its term is five years.
The Council of States: the upper House of Parliament, elected by State legislatures (plus 12 nominated); a permanent House where one-third retire every two years.
A State Legislative Assembly, directly elected for five years.
The upper House in a State that has one (Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Bihar, UP); created or abolished by Parliament under Art. 169.
The head of district administration (an IAS officer), responsible for revenue, law and order (as District Magistrate) and development.
In Andhra Pradesh, the administrative unit between the village and the district (since 1985, replacing taluks), headed by a Tahsildar; also the Mandal Praja Parishad.
The revenue officer in charge of a mandal or taluk.
The district-level body of the three-tier Panchayati Raj system.
By virtue of holding an office: for example, the Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
On its own motion: when a court or body acts without anyone filing a case.
A case filed in court for the public good by any person, even if not personally affected; developed by Justices Bhagwati and Krishna Iyer in the late 1970s-80s.
The anti-corruption ombudsman for the Centre under the Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act 2013, covering even the Prime Minister with safeguards.
The anti-corruption ombudsman of a State; Maharashtra was the first to set one up (1971).
A body set up to settle disputes in special areas (tax, service matters, environment) outside the regular courts (Arts. 323A and 323B).
The Centre and States working together on shared goals (for example through the GST Council and NITI Aayog).
States competing with each other to attract investment and improve governance, encouraged through rankings by NITI Aayog and DPIIT.

Extra central help (90:10 funding of central schemes, tax breaks) once given to hilly, border or poor States on the Gadgil formula; ended for new States after the 14th Finance Commission. Andhra Pradesh was promised it in 2014.
